title: Is the change real? Test noise in practice
goal: Use the typical errors of common tests and the smallest worthwhile change to decide whether an athlete's result really changed, and plan testing so that real change can be seen.

steps.title: How noisy is each test?
steps.text:
*Noise, worthwhile changes and non-responders* gave the tools; here are the [typical errors](g:typical-error) of this module's tests:

| test | typical error (CV) |
|---|---|
| ramp peak power or speed | ~0.9% [[c:ppo-cv]] |
| 20-min TT ([FTP](g:ftp)) | 1.3–2.9% [[c:ftp-cv]] |
| lactate-threshold power | ~1.5% pooled; 3.4–3.7% in one cyclist study, Dmax 10.3% [[c:lt-cv]] |
| field CP from 3 efforts | 2.4–6.5% (last lesson) |
| [VO2max](g:vo2max) | ~5.6% (evidence module) |

Power worked out from gas was 1.4–1.6 times noisier than ergometer power [[c:resp-noisier]].

Why is Dmax so noisy? A likely reason: its line runs to the last point of the test, so it moves with how hard the athlete pushes the final stage.

claims.text: Peak power in an incremental test on a treadmill or cycle ergometer has a typical error of about 0.9%.

evidence.quote: peak power in an incremental test on a treadmill or cycle ergometer (approximately 0.9%)

claims.text: A 20-min time trial for FTP repeated with a CV of 2.9% in 25 trained cyclists; in 8 trained men, its typical error was 4.6 W at about 343 W (about 1.3%). Pooled across studies, mean power in tests of 1 min to 3 h has a typical error of 0.9–2.0%.

evidence.quote: The results show that the 20-min time-trial was reliable (CV=2.9%, ICC=0.97), despite a less reliable warm-up (CV=5.5%, ICC=0.84).
equivalent mean power in a constant-power test lasting 1 minute to 3 hours on a treadmill or cycle ergometer (0.9 to 2.0%)

claims.text: Pooled across studies, lactate-threshold power has a typical error of about 1.5%; in 14 trained male cyclists it repeated with a CV of 3.4–3.7%, except for the Dmax method (CV 10.3%).

evidence.quote: Lactate threshold tests had high reliability (CV = 3.4-3.7%; r = 0.85-0.89; Bias = -2.1-3.0) except for DMAX method (CV = 10.3%; r = 0.57; Bias = 15.4).

claims.text: Respiratory-based measures of power had CVs 1.4–1.6 times larger than ergometer-based measures.

evidence.quote: respiratory- versus ergometer-based measures of power (1.4 to 1.6 x)

steps.title: A high ICC, and still noisy
steps.text:
Many reliability papers report an [ICC](g:icc), a retest [correlation](g:correlation). The 20-min FTP test above had an ICC of **0.97** and a CV of **2.9%** [[c:ftp-icc]]. The ICC looks almost perfect; the CV says a 280 W rider can swing by about 8 W with no real change.

The ICC depends on how different the people in the study are. A group mixing novices and pros gives a high ICC even with a noisy test, because the gaps between people dwarf the noise [[c:icc-spread]].

So the ICC tells you whether a test ranks a group; the typical error tells you whether one athlete changed.

claims.text: The 20-min FTP time trial had an ICC of 0.97 with a CV of 2.9% in 25 trained cyclists.

evidence.quote: The results show that the 20-min time-trial was reliable (CV=2.9%, ICC=0.97)

claims.text: Retest correlation is hard to interpret because it is sensitive to how heterogeneous the sample is; the typical error is the better standard measure of reliability.

evidence.quote: Retest correlation is difficult to interpret, mainly because its value is sensitive to the heterogeneity of the sample of participants.
A wider understanding of reliability and adoption of the typical error as the standard measure of reliability would improve the assessment of tests and equipment in our disciplines.

steps.title: Noise band first, then the SWC
steps.text:
For one athlete, start with the 95% noise band from the evidence module: about **±2.8 × typical error** for a single retest. A change outside it is probably real.

Then ask whether it matters: is it bigger than the [smallest worthwhile change](g:smallest-worthwhile-change)? For an elite athlete's race result, the SWC is about 0.3 of race-to-race variation [[c:swc-03]]. For team-sport tests, with no direct link to a result, the default is **0.2 × the between-athlete [SD](g:standard-deviation)**, a small [Cohen's d](g:cohens-d) [[c:swc-02]]. This course borrows that default for lab markers such as threshold power: an assumption, not a tested rule.

In most performance tests the noise is bigger than the SWC [[c:noise-bigger]], so one retest rarely settles a small change.

claims.text: For elite athletes competing as individuals, the smallest worthwhile enhancement is about 0.3 of an athlete's typical competition-to-competition variation (~0.3–1% of power output, depending on the sport).

evidence.quote: the required change in performance is 0.3 of the typical variation in an athlete's performance from competition to competition, or ~0.3-1% when expressed as a change in power output, depending on the sport.

claims.text: Where test performance has no direct relationship with competition performance, a default smallest worthwhile change is 0.2 of the between-athlete SD (Cohen effect size 0.20).

evidence.quote: In team sports, where there is no direct relationship between team and test performance, an appropriate default for the smallest change in test performance is one-fifth of the between-athlete standard deviation (a standardized or Cohen effect size of 0.20).

claims.text: The noise in most performance tests is greater than the smallest worthwhile change, which makes assessing changes problematic.

evidence.quote: The noise in most performance tests is greater than the smallest worthwhile difference, so assessments of changes in performance can be problematic.

steps.title: Is a threshold gain real, and does it matter?
steps.problem: A cyclist's lactate-threshold power rises from 250 W to 265 W (+6%). The test's typical error is 3.5%. In her squad, the between-athlete SD of threshold power is 30 W.
steps: Noise band for one retest: 2.8 × 3.5% ≈ ±9.8%. A 6% change sits inside it: this pair of tests can't confirm it.
SWC, using the 0.2 × SD default borrowed from team sports: 0.2 × 30 W = 6 W. The change, 15 W, is bigger than the SWC: if it is real, it matters.
Verdict: worth having, not yet proven. Retest, or average two tests (next card).

steps.title: Making change visible
steps.text:
When the noise beats the SWC, change the testing, not the verdict:

- **Average repeats.** The typical error of the mean of n tests is TE ÷ √n: two 20-min tests cut 2.9% to 2.1%.
- **Practise first.** A familiarisation trial before the baseline (evidence module).
- **Standardise.** Everything in this module: protocol, device, [averaging interval](g:averaging-interval), diet, weather.
- **Know where the noise lives.** In repeated cart tests of trained cyclists, about 60–70% of the VO₂ variability came from the athlete and 30–40% from the equipment, in one small study [[c:bio-tech]]. Better kit helps, but much of the noise is you.

Performance and physiological measures were also far steadier than hormonal ones: critical differences of about 12% against 60% [[c:bagger]].

claims.text: In repeated human testing, biological variability accounted for about 60–70% of VO₂ variability and technological variability for about 30–40%.

evidence.quote: Biological and technological V̇O2 and V̇CO2 variability, respectively, accounted for ~60%-70% and 40%-30% of the variability in repeated human testing.

claims.text: In 15 moderately trained male runners, performance and physiological variables had the lowest critical difference (11.9%), metabolic and hormonal variables the highest (59.9%).

evidence.quote: In the performance and physiological variables, 78.9 % of the variance was due to variation between subjects and they had the lowest critical difference (11.9 %). In contrast, the metabolic and hormonal variables had the highest critical difference (59.9 %)

steps.title: Three time trials instead of one
steps.problem: A runner's 5 km time trial has a typical error of 1.5%. How noisy is the average of 3 time trials, and what noise band does a change between two such averages carry?
steps: Typical error of a mean of 3 = 1.5% ÷ √3 = 1.5 ÷ 1.73 = 0.87%.
Noise band for a change between two averages = ±2.8 × 0.87% ≈ ±2.4%.
For single time trials it would be ±2.8 × 1.5% = ±4.2%. Three tests each time cut the band by about 40% (÷ √3).

points: Typical errors differ a lot: ramp peak power ~0.9%, 20-min TT 1.3–2.9%, lactate-threshold power ~1.5% pooled to 3.7% (Dmax 10%), field CP 2.4–6.5%, VO2max ~5.6%.
A high ICC can hide a noisy test: it rises with the spread between people. For one athlete, use the typical error.
Decide in two steps: is the change outside ±2.8 × typical error, and is it bigger than the SWC (here 0.2 × between-athlete SD, a default borrowed from team sports)?
Averaging n tests divides the typical error by √n; practice trials and strict standardisation cut noise further.
In one small study most VO₂ test noise came from the athlete, not the equipment, so even a perfect cart can't make one retest decisive.

variants.stem: In trained cyclists, Dmax threshold power repeated far worse (CV 10.3%) than other lactate thresholds (about 3.5%). Most likely reason?

options.text: Its line ends at the last point, set by how hard the athlete pushes
options.why: Right: Dmax uses the line from the first to the last point, so a stronger or weaker final stage moves the threshold.

options.text: It needs far more blood samples than other methods
options.why: Dmax uses the same samples as the other methods; it just reads them differently.

options.text: It uses a fixed 4 mmol·L⁻¹ value for everyone
options.why: That is OBLA; Dmax uses the shape of the curve, not a fixed value.

options.text: It can only be measured with a lab analyser
options.why: Any analyser works; the noise comes from the method's dependence on the end of the test.

variants.stem: You want to detect a 3% gain in a trained cyclist from a single retest. Which test gives you a chance? (Noise band ≈ ±2.8 × typical error.)

options.text: Ramp peak power, same protocol
options.why: Right: 2.8 × 0.9% ≈ ±2.5%, so a 3% change can stand out.

options.text: A 20-min FTP test
options.why: With a 2.9% typical error, the band is about ±8%: a 3% gain hides inside it.

options.text: Lactate-threshold power
options.why: With about 3.5% typical error, the band is about ±10%.

options.text: A VO2max test
options.why: With about 5.6% typical error, the band is about ±16%.

variants.solution: Noise band = 2.8 × typical error: peak power 2.8 × 0.9 ≈ 2.5%; FTP 2.8 × 2.9 ≈ 8.1%; lactate threshold 2.8 × 3.5 ≈ 9.8%; VO2max 2.8 × 5.6 ≈ 16%. Only peak power's band is smaller than 3%.

variants.stem: Test A has an ICC of 0.98 and a CV of 4%. Test B has an ICC of 0.90 and a CV of 1.5%. Which is better for tracking one triathlete?

options.text: Test B, because its typical error is smaller
options.why: Right: for one athlete, the noise that matters is the typical error, and B's is less than half of A's.

options.text: Test A, because its ICC is higher
options.why: A higher ICC can come from a more varied study group, not a less noisy test.

options.text: Either: both have an ICC above 0.9
options.why: An ICC above 0.9 says nothing about whether a test can track one athlete's small changes.

options.text: Neither: only an ICC of 1.0 is good enough
options.why: No real test reaches 1.0; the question is whether the typical error is small enough.

variants.stem: Two running tests: X has an ICC of 0.99 and a CV of 3%; Y has an ICC of 0.92 and a CV of 1%. Which is better for spotting a 2% change in one runner?

options.text: Y, because its typical error is smaller
options.why: Right: Y's noise band is about ±2.8%, X's about ±8.4%; only Y comes close to a 2% change.

options.text: X, because its ICC is higher
options.why: A higher ICC can come from a more varied study group, not a less noisy test.

options.text: Either: both have an ICC above 0.9
options.why: An ICC above 0.9 says nothing about whether a test can track one runner's small changes.

options.text: Neither: only lab tests can spot 2%
options.why: What matters is a test's typical error, not where it is run.

variants.stem: A study of club riders and professionals together reports an ICC of 0.99 for a new test. Why might that flatter the test?

options.text: The big gaps between riders inflate the ICC
options.why: Right: the ICC rises with how different the people are, so a mixed group makes even a noisy test look reliable.

options.text: Professionals make every test more accurate
options.why: Athletes are less noisy than non-athletes, but that isn't why a mixed group inflates the ICC.

options.text: An ICC above 0.95 is always a statistical error
options.why: High ICCs are common and can be correct; the issue is what they measure.

options.text: The ICC measures the average gain, not the noise
options.why: The ICC is a retest correlation, not a measure of change; it isn't about gains at all.

variants.stem: A cyclist's 20-min test (typical error 2.9%) goes from 270 to 290 W (+7.4%). Is the change real?

options.text: Can't confirm it: the noise band is about ±8.1%
options.why: Right: 2.8 × 2.9% ≈ 8.1%, and 7.4% sits just inside.

options.text: Real: 7.4% is bigger than the 2.9% typical error
options.why: This compares the change with one test's noise; a change between two tests carries √2 more, and a 95% band × 1.96.

options.text: Real: 7.4% beats the 4.1% noise on a change
options.why: √2 × 2.9% = 4.1% is one SD of the change; the 95% band also needs × 1.96.

options.text: Can't confirm it: any change under 10% is noise
options.why: There's no fixed cut-off: the band depends on the test's typical error.

variants.solution: Noise band = 2.8 × typical error = 2.8 × 2.9% ≈ ±8.1% (that is 1.96 × √2 × 2.9%). +7.4% is inside it, so one retest can't confirm the gain.

variants.stem: A runner's treadmill ramp peak speed (typical error 0.9%) rises by 4% with the same protocol. Is the change real?

options.text: Probably real: outside the ±2.5% noise band
options.why: Right: 2.8 × 0.9% ≈ 2.5%, and 4% is outside it.

options.text: Can't confirm it: inside the ±8% noise band
options.why: That band belongs to a test with a 2.9% typical error, such as the 20-min test, not to ramp peak speed.

options.text: Can't confirm it: inside the ±14% noise band
options.why: That band belongs to a test with a 5% typical error, close to VO2max's, not to peak speed.

options.text: Can't confirm it: one retest can never show change
options.why: One retest can show a change when it is clearly bigger than the noise, as here.

variants.solution: Noise band = 2.8 × 0.9% ≈ ±2.5%. A 4% rise is outside it, so it is probably real.

variants.stem: A triathlete's VO2max (typical error 5%) goes from 4.0 to 4.3 L·min⁻¹ (+7.5%). Is the change real?

options.text: Can't confirm it: the noise band is about ±14%
options.why: Right: 2.8 × 5% = 14%, and 7.5% is well inside.

options.text: Real: 7.5% is bigger than the 5% typical error
options.why: This compares the change with one test's noise; a change between two tests carries √2 more, and a 95% band × 1.96.

options.text: Real: 7.5% beats the 7.1% noise on a change
options.why: √2 × 5% = 7.1% is one SD of the change; the 95% band also needs × 1.96.

options.text: Real: a lab cart has almost no noise
options.why: VO2max varies about 5–6% between tests, mostly from the athlete, not the cart.

variants.solution: Noise band = 2.8 × 5% = ±14%. +7.5% is inside it, so this pair of tests can't confirm the gain.

variants.stem: In a squad of runners, threshold speed has a between-athlete SD of 1.0 km·h⁻¹. Using the 0.2 × SD default, what is the smallest worthwhile change?

options.text: 0.2 km·h⁻¹
0.3 km·h⁻¹
options.why: 0.3 is the factor for race-to-race variation, applied here to the between-athlete SD by mistake.

options.text: 0.5 km·h⁻¹
options.why: 0.5 SD is Cohen's 'medium' effect, not the smallest worthwhile one.

options.text: 1.0 km·h⁻¹
options.why: That is the SD itself, five times the default SWC.

variants.stem: In a group of cyclists, VO2max has a between-athlete SD of 6 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Using the 0.2 × SD default, what is the smallest worthwhile change?

options.text: 1.2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: Right: 0.2 × 6 = 1.2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹.

options.text: 1.8 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: This uses 0.3, the factor for race-to-race variation, on the between-athlete SD.

options.text: 3.0 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: 0.5 SD is Cohen's 'medium' effect, not the smallest worthwhile one.

options.text: 6.0 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: That is the SD itself, five times the default SWC.

variants.stem: A cyclist's 20-min test has a typical error of 2.9%. What is the typical error of the average of two such tests?

options.text: About 2.1%
About 1.45%
options.why: This divides by n (2) instead of √n: averaging helps, but less than that.

options.text: About 4.1%
options.why: This multiplies by √2, which is the noise on a change between two tests, not on their average.

options.text: 2.9%, unchanged
options.why: Averaging cancels some of the random noise, so the mean is less noisy than one test.

variants.solution: Typical error of a mean of n tests = TE ÷ √n = 2.9% ÷ √2 = 2.9 ÷ 1.41 ≈ 2.1%.

variants.stem: A runner's VO2max test has a typical error of 5%. What is the typical error of the average of four tests?

options.why: This divides by n (4) instead of √n (2).
This multiplies by √4 instead of dividing.

options.text: 5%, unchanged
options.why: Averaging cancels some of the random noise, so the mean is less noisy than one test.

variants.solution: Typical error of a mean of n tests = TE ÷ √n = 5% ÷ √4 = 5% ÷ 2 = 2.5%.

variants.stem: When trained cyclists repeat a steady-ride VO₂ test on a lab cart, where does most of the variation between days come from?

options.text: The athlete's own day-to-day variation
options.why: Right: about 60–70% of the VO₂ variability was biological, 30–40% technological.

options.text: The cart's sensors and analysers
options.why: The equipment adds about 30–40%: real, but the smaller share.

options.text: Errors in typing up the results
options.why: Transcription errors aren't the source studied; the split was between body and kit.

options.text: None: VO₂ is the same every day
options.why: Repeated tests always vary; the question is how much and why.

variants.stem: A study reports that a supplement raised VO2max by 3% in 10 cyclists, from one test before and one after, with no control group, on a test with a 5% typical error. What most limits it?

options.text: A 3% change against 5% noise, and no control for learning or chance
options.why: Right: a 3% mean change is small for a 5% test with 10 people, and without a control group a learning effect or regression to the mean could produce it.

options.text: VO2max should have been reported in mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
options.why: Units don't change whether the effect is real; the design does.

options.text: Nothing, as long as the result reached p < 0.05
options.why: A p-value doesn't remove the need for a control group or for familiarisation.

options.text: It tested cyclists, so it says nothing about runners
options.why: The sport limits who the result applies to, but the bigger problem is the design.
